passage: John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage
text: The narrator says her husband John laughs at her, and treats this as an ordinary part of married life. The selected line sits in the opening section of the story, where the narrator is describing why she suspects the house is strange and her husband dismisses her feelings. Her remark that "one expects that in marriage" is wry and resigned: she accepts his mockery as a normal feature of their relationship rather than a rare insult, which hints at the imbalance between them. The line also establishes John as a practical physician who doubts her imaginings, a dynamic that shapes the rest of the story p. 1. Her tone signals that she is already uneasy about being dismissed, even before the wallpaper becomes the focus.

passage: I am sitting by the window now, up in this atrocious nursery
text:
The narrator is sitting by a window in the upstairs nursery, which she calls "atrocious" because of its hideous wallpaper and worn furnishings. This is the room John has chosen for her, despite her wishes.

She is writing while her husband John is away at work, and she is clearly taking advantage of the solitude. The word "atrocious" signals her distaste for the room from the start, a feeling that will grow into the story's central obsession with the yellow wallpaper.

The line also shows the narrator's confinement: she is not free to choose her own surroundings, and writing in secret is one of the few things she can do on her own terms.

passage: Personally, I disagree with their ideas
text:
The narrator's disagreement with her doctors rests only on her own belief that work would help, which the story never tests against any evidence.

Her claim that congenial work would do her good is asserted rather than supported, and the document offers nothing beyond her own word to back it. Within page 1 she admits that "John says the very worst thing I can do is to think about my condition," and her doctors' view is presented as the expert judgment she must defer to. A critic could argue her self-diagnosis is itself unreliable, since she describes herself as unusually sensitive and prone to fancy. The author's reply, drawn from the story as a whole, is that the narrator's disagreement is meant to be read as a sign of the very condition her husband and brother describe, though this rests on later pages I should not draw on here.

passage: I have locked the door and thrown the key down into the front path
question: Why does she throw the key away?
text:
She says it herself in the next lines: "I don't want to go out, and I don't want to have anybody come in, till John comes. I want to astonish him." p. 12 So the key serves two purposes. It keeps Jennie and the servants from interrupting her work on the paper, and it lets her stay uninterrupted until John arrives and sees what she has done.

The document doesn't go further than that, so the rest is interpretation. Earlier she locks the door when she creeps by daylight, because she doesn't want to be seen p. 10. Throwing the key away makes that privacy permanent and removes the option of being persuaded out. She also says she won't go outside "even if Jennie asks me to" p. 12, which suggests she is choosing confinement, not just guarding against intruders.

The key also matters on the next page. Because it is outside, she can tell John it is "under a plantain leaf" and he has to go and fetch it, which gives her time p. 13.

Before you start
×

A woman, confined by her physician husband to a rented summer mansion for a supposed nervous condition, keeps a secret journal. Her fixation on the yellow wallpaper of her nursery room grows as the story moves through the summer.

Where we are

A couple rent a secluded colonial mansion for the summer; the narrator is forbidden to work and told to rest because of her "nervous depression." p. 1
They live in a former nursery at the top of the house, with barred windows, a bed fixed in place and peeling, repellent yellow wallpaper. p. 2
The narrator writes in secret, since her husband and his sister disapprove. The rental runs three months, so time is limited. p. 7

People

The narrator — Unnamed writer of the journal, a wife and new mother, treated as an invalid and cut off from work and company.
John — Her husband, a practical physician who dismisses her fears and directs her every hour.
Jennie — John's sister, a devoted housekeeper who looks after the household and the narrator.
Mary — The nurse who cares for the narrator's baby.
Her brother — Also a physician, who agrees with John's diagnosis of her condition.

Threads to watch

Her own sense of her illness and need for meaningful work clashes with the rest cure her husband and brother insist on. p. 1
The wallpaper's pattern, and a figure behind it, take over her attention. Watch how her account of what she sees changes. p. 7
She hides her writing, her wakefulness and her thoughts from John, while he and Jennie seem increasingly watchful of her. p. 8
The narrator's trust in John is strained as she asks to leave and is refused, with the lease ending in weeks. p. 7

question: Who is Jennie and how does she treat the narrator?
text:
The document never says exactly who Jennie is. She is first named as the person who "sees to everything now" p. 5, and John says she will get the house ready after the lease ends p. 7. That resembles the role of John's sister, introduced as "a perfect, and enthusiastic housekeeper" p. 4, but the document never says they are the same person. The narrator's last words, "in spite of you and Jane" p. 13, add a name the document doesn't explain, so any link is my inference.

Jennie's behavior is considerate. She is "good and lets me alone when I want her to" p. 5, she offers to sleep in the room with the narrator p. 11, and she tells her not to tire herself p. 11.

The narrator reads all of this as hostile. She notes Jennie's "inexplicable look" p. 8 and catches her with a hand on the paper, where Jennie explains that it stains clothing yellow p. 9. She also resents that Jennie reports her daytime sleeping to John p. 11. From the narrator's account alone, Jennie looks like a caring, watchful caretaker whom the narrator increasingly distrusts.
